Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rural police stations in Zambia predominantly use entirely paper-based systems for recording criminal cases and complaints. Baseline studies (2020) show 85.2% of police stations map crimes using physical maps and pins, with all stations processing crime reports manually into occurrence books, registers, and dockets; no digital entry at point of service. Paper forms are filled for complaints, witness statements, case dockets, police bonds, etc. Recent efforts (2026) by SMART Zambia to equip 40 stations with networking gear for centralized digital systems indicate ongoing pilots or upgrades, but these are nascent and not yet standard. Challenges include poor rural ICT infrastructure, low officer computer skills (24% trained), electricity/power issues, transport shortages, and manual data aggregation at higher levels. National ambitions for e-policing (proposed systems like cloud crime mapping, ZPS platform) and digital transformation (GMIS, e-learning) exist, but rural point-of-care remains paper-reliant, with data likely transcribed later at district levels. No evidence majority of rural stations use digital routinely; isolated national-level tools (AFIS fingerprints) do not extend to case recording. Score 1 reflects entirely paper at rural facilities despite policy pushes.

revision_notes: Original cited sources (2015-2016 University of Zambia papers) were fetched and confirmed relevant, describing a 2015 baseline where all surveyed stations processed crime reports manually. A fresh, more current source was fetched and read: a 2026 peer-reviewed study (Botha & Malisase, African Journal of Empirical Research) based on interviews conducted through December 2024, which finds that as of 2024 'key police services had not yet been digitised at ZPSHQ, and the entire ZPS' and that the Arrest and Prisoners Property Book, Occurrence Book, Crime Register Book and Docket Movement Book 'are all recorded manually and in paper form' nationwide, including in headquarters, implying rural stations (which lag HQ in ICT capacity) remain paper-based. A 2024 IOM project introduced an Electronic Occurrence Book (E-OB) pilot only at Chipata stations, and a February 2026 SMART Zambia rollout is delivering networking hardware (routers, switches) to 40 stations as infrastructure groundwork, not yet operational digital record capture. No authoritative source shows routine digital data capture in rural police stations. Score of 1 (Entirely paper) is confirmed, now resting on evidence current to 2024-2026 rather than only 2015-2016 baseline studies.
revised_comments: Rural police stations in Zambia continue to record cases entirely on paper. A 2026 peer-reviewed study covering the Zambia Police Service through 2024 finds that reporting of cases, recording of statements and the opening of case dockets are still done manually and physically, with the Arrest and Prisoners Property Book, Occurrence Book, Crime Register Book and Docket Movement Book all recorded manually and in paper form nationwide, a pattern more pronounced away from headquarters. A single pilot Electronic Occurrence Book exists at Chipata police stations, and in early 2026 SMART Zambia began delivering networking equipment (routers, switches, access points) to 40 stations under the Police Service Local Area Network and Last Mile Connectivity Project, laying groundwork for future digitisation. This infrastructure has not yet translated into digital data capture at the point of service in rural stations, which remain reliant on manual books and paper dockets.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Zambia predominantly use paper-based registers and tally sheets for patient data recording at the point of service. Data is aggregated monthly on paper reports and submitted to district offices for entry into DHIS2, the national HMIS platform.Health Policy and Planning 2023 Patient details are often recorded twice: in paper health passports and facility registers.Zambia HIS Assessment 2007 Digital systems like SmartCare (EHR) and DHIS2 exist nationally, with SmartCare Pro rolled out to 877 facilities (of 3,540 total) as of 2025, but most rural clinics lack computers, reliable power, and internet, remaining paper-based.Global Fund Zambia Digital Health 2025 Pilots like CHIP for community health workers (2025) and limited SmartCare in select rural antenatal sites indicate some digital adoption, but not widespread at clinics.PATH article Key barriers include frequent power outages (hydro-dependent grid), poor rural connectivity, staff shortages, overwhelming registers (21+ per small facility), and flooding/transport issues delaying submissions. National ambitions (Digital Health Strategy 2022-2026, SmartCare expansion) outpace rural reality, where paper persists despite aggregation-level digitalization. Score 2: digital limited to pilots/district entry, not routine point-of-service.

revision_notes: Original cited sources were fetched: the 2023 Health Policy and Planning qualitative study (Western Province) and the April 2025 Global Fund case study, both of which support the description of paper-first, aggregated-later HMIS reporting and describe rural facility power/connectivity constraints. Fresh searches confirm the SmartCare Pro EHR rollout reached 400 facilities by August 2024 (SMART Zambia Institute) with plans to extend to 600, and combined with legacy SmartCare versions covers roughly 1,800 of Zambia's health facilities as of 2025 - a large expansion, but still a minority of the roughly 3,540 total facilities, and concentrated where power and connectivity have been secured. An October 2025 UNDP/SMART Zambia/Ministry of Health partnership is still in the process of extending solar power and connectivity to rural and peri-urban clinics precisely because these are the facilities most often left on paper systems. No authoritative source indicates that most rural primary clinics have moved beyond paper registers at the point of care. Score of 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) is confirmed, updated to reflect 2024-2025 rollout figures rather than the 2007 assessment previously cited alongside newer sources.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Zambia predominantly record patient data on paper registers and tally sheets at the point of care, with aggregated data later entered into DHIS2 at district level. The government's SmartCare Pro electronic health record system had reached 400 facilities by August 2024, with plans to expand further, and SmartCare in its various versions now covers around 1,800 of the country's roughly 3,540 health facilities as of 2025, concentrated where solar power and internet connectivity have been secured. A partnership between the Ministry of Health, the Smart Zambia Institute and UNDP, formalised in October 2025, is actively extending solar power and digital connectivity to rural and peri-urban facilities that currently lack them, underscoring that most rural clinics still lack the infrastructure for routine digital data capture and remain reliant on paper records supplemented by pilot digital systems.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in Zambia primarily use paper-based systems for birth registration, with manual records leading to low coverage (9% rural births registered per 2007 ZDHS; overall <15% as of 2024 per UNICEF).WHO Zambia CRVS Plan 2015, [BiometricUpdate 2025] Digital efforts include the national INRIS platform (launched ~2022, scaled to 40+ districts), decentralization of certification to district levels (SI 44/2016), mobile registration units with digital tools for remote areas (UNICEF/World Vision), and plans for full digitization/integration with health systems (CRVS Policy 2022).[OHCHR subm.], [UNECA digital CRVS] However, no evidence shows majority rural facilities routinely use digital at point-of-service; rural lags urban in performance, with infrastructure gaps (electricity, internet, staffing), low awareness, distance, poverty as barriers.[WHO Plan], [OHCHR] National ambitions (50% registration by 2026, digital ID 2027) outpace rural reality, where paper remains default and digital is limited to pilots/outreach, not standard POS.

revision_notes: Original cited sources (2015 WHO CRVS strategic plan, OHCHR submission, UNECA CRVS digitalisation report) were fetched; they support the description of low rural birth-registration coverage and paper-based default but pre-date the INRIS rollout. Fresh searches find that as of December 2025, roughly 1.3 million citizens have been enrolled on the Integrated National Registration Information System (INRIS) with over 500,000 births and deaths registered (ZNBC), and the Ministry of Home Affairs describes ongoing efforts to 'decentralize the process and bring it close to remote communities' (Biometric Update, August 2025), implying this has not yet been achieved. A December 2025 peer-reviewed study of Kabwe District confirms only 50 of Zambia's 116 districts have the capacity to issue birth certificates, and cites UNICEF (2024) data showing rural birth registration coverage of just 9.5% compared to 25.5% in urban areas nationally 14% overall. INRIS deployment documentation shows initial enrolment concentrated in 11 (mostly urban/provincial-capital) districts. No authoritative evidence indicates most rural registry offices have moved to routine digital point-of-service registration. Score of 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) is confirmed, updated with 2025 figures.
revised_comments: Rural civil registry offices in Zambia continue to rely predominantly on paper-based processes for birth, death and marriage registration. The government's Integrated National Registration Information System (INRIS) had enrolled around 1.3 million citizens and recorded over 500,000 births and deaths by December 2025, but deployment remains concentrated in a limited number of mostly urban and provincial-capital districts, with only 50 of the country's 116 districts able to issue birth certificates. The Ministry of Home Affairs and Internal Security has explicitly identified decentralising registration to remote communities as a forward-looking goal rather than an accomplished one. National birth registration coverage stood at around 14% in 2024, with rural coverage of roughly 9.5% compared with 25.5% in urban areas, reflecting the continued reliance on manual, paper-based registration in rural facilities alongside a digital system that is being rolled out but has yet to reach most rural registry offices at the point of service.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Zambia predominantly use paper-based registers for daily administrative data like attendance and learning outcomes, as evidenced by biometric pilots replacing inaccurate paper systems and descriptions of annual census data as outdated. The Ministry of Education's EMIS relies on annual school census data collected via CS Pro 7.7 tool deployed electronically to schools, indicating some digital entry at school level during census periods, but not routine point-of-service use. Pilots like Akros DHIS2 in Namwala district and Simprints biometrics in 8 rural eastern schools introduce digital tracking for attendance and aggregates, supported by UNICEF/World Bank projects aiming to strengthen EMIS, but these are isolated/district-level, not majority coverage. Barriers include poor rural infrastructure (electricity, internet, devices), low teacher digital capacity, and reliance on annual aggregates over real-time data. National policy pushes digital migration (e.g., 2024 ESB describes shift from paper), but rural reality lags with paper default and digital limited to pilots/periodic reporting.Ministry of Education Zambia 2024 ESB; Simprints rural Zambia schools case study; Akros Zambia EMIS pilot

revision_notes: The Ministry of Education Statistics Bulletin 2024 PDF could not be fetched directly (403 error on the government server), but its substance is corroborated by other sources. The Simprints case study (fetched, December 2024) and a January 2025 American Institutes for Research endline evaluation of the Impact Network eSchool 360 programme (fetched) both confirm that in the 8 participating rural eastern Zambia schools, teachers still track attendance daily through a paper register, with data only entered into the CommCare digital system on a weekly basis - i.e. paper remains the point-of-service tool with digital capture happening after the fact. The Akros/DHIS2 EMIS pilot (fetched) remains confined to Namwala district, replacing what was previously an annual paper-based census system with monthly digital aggregate reporting, but is not evidence of national rural coverage. A 2024 Global Partnership for Education compact document confirms the national EMIS still needs 'tools to upgrade and automate' data collection, indicating the national system remains a work in progress. No authoritative source indicates that rural primary schools nationally have moved beyond paper attendance and administrative registers at the point of service. Score of 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) is confirmed, now resting on 2024-2025 evidence.
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Zambia predominantly rely on paper registers for daily attendance and administrative record-keeping at the point of service, with the Ministry of Education's national Education Management Information System still dependent chiefly on periodic school census returns rather than real-time facility-level digital capture. Isolated pilots demonstrate a path toward digitisation: in Namwala district, Akros and the Ministry of General Education, with UNICEF support, replaced annual paper census reporting with a DHIS2-based monthly digital reporting tool, and in eight rural eastern Zambia schools operating under the Impact Network eSchool 360 model, Simprints biometric fingerprint scanning has improved attendance-data accuracy, although teachers still complete a daily paper register first and data is only uploaded to the CommCare digital system on a weekly basis. These initiatives remain confined to specific districts and school networks rather than representing standard practice, so most rural primary schools continue to default to paper-based data capture supplemented by limited digital pilots and periodic digital aggregation.
